proof:
# Grouped positive normals do not minimize every reflected simplex pair

Let T_d=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d), V_d=|T_d|, R=1, and t=1/(d+1).
For r<=1 and a nonnegative continuous normal u with sum u_i=1,
write

    F_(u,r)(h)=|rT_d intersect {u.x>=h}|/V_d.

The reflected-pair cost with opposite shifts is

    F_(u,r)(t-s)+F_(u,r)(t+s),   s>=0.            (1)

A proposed extremal restriction is to normals having k equal positive
coordinates and d-k zero coordinates. It is FALSE already in d=3.
Section 1 gives an exact certificate against every normal in that
class and every opposite shift. Section 2 gives the exact replacement
optimization in the narrower zero-shift, one-vertex-cap sector.
No universal all-normal two-level extremality, or OC consequence,
is asserted.

## 1. Exact d=3 countercertificate

Take d=3, r=9/10, t=1/4, and

    u=(5/9,2/9,2/9),    s=0.

Its three positive vertex heights are 1/2,1/5,1/5. The threshold
1/4 lies above the two smaller heights, so the cap is the simplex
at the largest-height vertex. Its exact volume divided by V_3 is

    (1/2-1/4)^3/[(5/9)(5/9-2/9)^2]=81/320.

Thus the pair in (1) costs exactly 81/160.

For a grouped normal with k positive coordinates, write
Y=X_1+...+X_k for a uniform point X in T_3. Its law is
Beta(k,4-k). This follows directly by slicing the simplex at that
coordinate sum: the section factor is proportional to
Y^(k-1)(1-Y)^(3-k). Since u.X=Y/k, set

    q=k t/r,    v=k s/r.

The pair cost divided by r^3 is the sum of the two upper tails of
Y at q-v and q+v. Permutations of a grouped normal have the same
law, so the following three cases exhaust the proposed class.

For k=1, q=5/18 and the tail is G(x)=(1-x)^3 on [0,1], clipped
to 1 and 0 outside. While v<=q, convexity of (1-x)_+^3 gives
the lower bound 2G(q), attained at v=0. If v>=q, the lower
threshold tail is 1, no smaller than 2G(q), since
2(13/18)^3<1. Hence its exact minimum, restoring r^3, is

    2(r-t)^3=2197/4000.

For k=2, q=5/9 and G(x)=1-3x^2+2x^3 on [0,1]. For
0<=v<=1-q both cuts lie in the support and the exact sum is

    G(q-v)+G(q+v)=2G(q)+(12q-6)v^2.

Its coefficient is positive. For v>=1-q the upper-threshold
tail is zero and the other tail increases as v increases, until
it is 1. Thus the exact minimum is at v=0, and its original
mass is

    r^3 2G(5/9)=608/1000.

For k=3, q=5/6 and G(x)=1-x^3 on [0,1]. For
0<=v<=1-q, the sum is 2-2q^3-6qv^2 and decreases. After
v=1-q the upper tail is zero and the other increases. The
minimum is at v=1/6 and has original mass

    r^3[1-(2q-1)^3]
      =r^3-(6t-r)^3=513/1000.

All clipping transitions, whole-cap regimes, and support boundaries
have been included. Consequently the least grouped-normal cost is
513/1000, whereas

    513/1000-81/160=27/4000>0.                   (2)

This strictly refutes the grouped-normal restriction. It is a
counterexample to that auxiliary restriction, not to (OC).

## 2. Exact two-level optimum for zero-shift one-vertex caps

Let d>=2 and

    d/(d+1)<r<=1,    t=1/(d+1),
    L=(d+1)r-d>0,
    D=d^2-(d^2-1)r=d-(d-1)L>0.

Among all nonnegative normals u with sum u_i=1 for which the
zero-shift cap {u.x>=t} of rT_d isolates just one positive
vertex (allowing other vertices on the cutting boundary), the
minimum single-cap mass divided by V_d is exactly

    Gamma_d L,     Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d.          (3)

It is attained by the two-level normal

    u_1=a_*=1/D,
    u_2=...=u_d=b_*=(d+1)(1-r)/D.               (4)

For r<1 the minimizer is unique up to permutation of the coordinates.
At r=1 it is a coordinate normal. The paired zero-shift value supplied
by (4) is 2Gamma_d L. This is an exact optimum only in the stated
one-vertex zero-shift sector, not over arbitrary shifts or cap types.

### Proof

Relabel so that u_1=a is the isolated vertex normal coefficient.
All other coefficients obey u_i r<=t<ar. The cap determinant gives

    F_(u,r)(t)=(ar-t)^d/[a product_(i=2)^d(a-u_i)]. (5)

For fixed a, arithmetic-geometric mean bounds the denominator by

    a[(da-1)/(d-1)]^(d-1),

with equality exactly when the other d-1 coefficients are equal.
Replacing them by their mean preserves nonnegativity and the
one-vertex condition because their mean is at most their maximum.
Thus the minimization reduces to

    f(a)=(ar-t)^d/[a((da-1)/(d-1))^(d-1)],
    1-(d-1)t/r<=a<=1.                           (6)

The lower endpoint exceeds both 1/d and t/r because r>dt.
On this whole interval all factors in (6) are strictly positive.
Direct logarithmic differentiation gives

    f'(a)/f(a)
      =dr/(ar-t)-1/a-d(d-1)/(da-1)
      =t(aD-1)/[a(ar-t)(da-1)].                 (7)

Thus f decreases before a=1/D and increases afterwards. This point
belongs to the allowed interval. Indeed D>=1 gives a_*<=1,
and its difference from the left endpoint is exactly

    a_*-[1-(d-1)t/r]=(d-1)L^2/[D(d+1)r]>=0.     (8)

The coefficient b_* in (4) is (1-a_*)/(d-1), and a_*-b_*=L/D.
In particular the selected largest vertex is unique. Also

    t-b_*r=L^2/[(d+1)D]>=0,                     (9)

which directly checks the one-vertex regime. Finally

    a_*r-t=dL/[(d+1)D],
    a_*(a_*-b_*)^(d-1)=L^(d-1)/D^d.

Substitution in (5) gives (3). Equation (7) and the strict equality
case of arithmetic-geometric mean prove uniqueness. For d=2 there
is only one smaller coefficient, so that equality condition is
automatic and uniqueness still follows from (7).

For 0<r<=d/(d+1), the all-equal positive normal u_i=1/d has its
largest height r/d<=t and hence zero cap volume. That zero regime
does not need the formula (4). The two-level optimum in (3) tends
continuously to zero at the transition but no limiting optimizer
is needed for the separate zero assertion.

At d=3,r=9/10, (4) gives a_*=5/9 and b_*=2/9 and (3) is 81/320,
recovering the countercertificate in Section 1. For a general R>0,
replace r by r/R throughout and multiply all volume expressions
by R^d; the normals themselves are unchanged by that scaling.

## 3. Relation to the already proved ordinary depth formula

The ordinary cap value (3) is also a direct consequence of the
previously proved `candidate 8704554a92158bfc`.
It is not a new ordinary simplex depth theorem. The point y=t(1,...,1)
in rT_d has barycentric coordinates

    lambda_0=(r-dt)/r,   lambda_i=t/r for 1<=i<=d.

For d/(d+1)<=r<=1 they all lie in [0,1/d], with lambda_0<=lambda_i.
The archived central-region formula therefore gives the GLOBAL
ordinary depth, allowing every normal, as

    r^d d^d lambda_0 (t/r)^(d-1) V_d
        =Gamma_d[(d+1)r-d] V_d.

The elementary derivation in Section 2 supplies its explicit positive
two-level minimizing normal and an independent calculation within
that cap regime. The remaining paired question is whether opposite
shifts can decrease the sum below twice this ordinary depth. The
countercertificate in Section 1 does not settle that question.
